html:
The closing document of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, signed in Helsinki, Finland, on 1 August 1975 by 35 states: every European country but Albania, plus the United States and Canada.

It was a high point of détente in the Cold War. The Soviet Union wanted the West to accept the borders drawn after the Second World War, and it got that. In return the East signed up to respect human rights and the free flow of people and ideas. Leaders in Moscow saw that part as words on paper.

Dissidents took the words seriously. Citizens set up watch groups to report abuses, starting with the Moscow Helsinki Group in 1976. Charter 77 in Czechoslovakia and later the Solidarity movement in Poland pointed to the same promises. The accords gave them a legal claim their governments had signed, and helped wear down the regimes that fell in 1989 with the Berlin Wall. The conference itself became the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe in 1995.
